stories.title: Designed broken symmetries facilitate configurational complexity in nematic vortex crystals
stories.description: Although widely used in modern technological applications, liquid crystals have not yet been systematically explored or utilized as reconfigurable information storage devices. Here we demonstrate that precisely designed broken symmetries in nematic vortex crystal lattices give rise to exponential configurational complexity exceeding the configurational entropy of conventional atomic crystals, and arising from the manifold ways in which surface-anchored nematic defect lines can combine to form nematic vortex crystals with distinct free-energy minima and tailored broken symmetries, thereby generalizing the interstitial and substitutional defects as well as grain boundaries in conventional crystalline materials. We illustrate the versatility of our experimental platform by designing nematic vortex crystals with various broken symmetries and show how their topological states can be reconfigured on demand via laser-induced topological surgery. Thus, our results provide an experimental and conceptual foundation for the development of soft-matter-based topological memory and computation devices. Hierarchical defects in nematic liquid crystals act as meta-atoms for the development of soft-matter-based topological memory and neuromorphic computation.

stories.title: PIC-NIC reveals that DNA mechanical strain impacts transcription factor recognition
stories.description: DNA is not merely a linear code of bases, but a mechanically constrained polymer whose backbone continuity restricts the conformations accessible during protein recognition. Yet, although base-sequence preferences have been extensively mapped across human transcription factor (TF) families, we lack comparable maps of how TFs read backbone continuity and DNA mechanics, leaving these layers of recognition poorly understood. Here we introduce PIC-NIC, a high-throughput platform that uses site-specific backbone nicks to perturb DNA mechanics while preserving base identity and minimizing accompanying chemical changes. Across 15 TFs spanning eight structural families, PIC-NIC reveals a highly position-dependent response to backbone disruption: most positions are permissive, whereas nicking at mechanically sensitive sites can substantially reshape binding. Mechanistic analyses integrating PIC-NIC maps with freshly determined TF–DNA structures, structural comparisons, binding kinetics and molecular simulations show that sensitive positions often coincide with strain-adapted DNA geometries, including Hoogsteen conformations, whose relaxation can enhance binding or rewire sequence specificity. Genomic single-strand breaks and repair maps further suggest that TF retention at nicked DNA may influence local repair-factor accessibility. Together, these findings systematically map DNA backbone mechanics as a position-resolved layer of TF recognition across diverse protein families, showing how this layer can reshape binding specificity and may influence repair-factor accessibility. Yao et al. develop PIC-NIC, a high-throughput platform using site-specific DNA nicks to systematically map how local mechanical strain shapes transcription factor recognition beyond DNA sequence alone across diverse protein–DNA interfaces.

stories.title: Targeted technology coadoption for reconciling energy savings and equity gains in the residential energy transition
stories.description: The transition to net-zero residential energy relies on the rapid integration of photovoltaics (PV), electric vehicles and heat pumps, yet their systemic interactions remain under-examined. Using machine learning across 17,900 households, we show that targeting energy use and cost reduction leads to technology allocation to traditional early adopters—wealthy, single-family homeowners, reinforcing spatial clustering. Conversely, aiming at minimizing population-wide energy burden produces a socio-demographic realignment, directing technologies to underserved households and yielding a more spatially dispersed distribution. PV deployment to these households leads to strong equity gains relative to electric vehicles or heat pumps. Promoting co-adoption further reduce energy burden. These results underscore the need for targeted, bundled support that extends beyond homeowner-centric models to deliver PV access and integrated technology portfolios to low-income renter and multi-family sectors. Targeting burden reduction realigns technology distribution towards disadvantaged households. The study shows that solar co-adoption for these households can deliver equity gains, highlighting the need for bundled, multifamily and renter-accessible policies.

stories.title: Structural basis of electron transfer by the human nitric oxide synthase holoenzyme complex
stories.description: Mammalian nitric oxide synthase (NOS) generates nitric oxide (NO), an essential signaling molecule in neurotransmission, inflammation and cardiovascular regulation. NOS dysregulation contributes to neurodegeneration, septic shock and ischemia. The structural basis of NOS function remains unclear, likely because of its dynamic, multicomponent architecture. Catalysis requires electron transfer across five cofactors, with the oxygenase (Oxy) domain converting l-arginine to NO after receiving electrons from the reductase (Red) domain through calmodulin (CaM) activation. Here, we report cryo-electron microscopy structures of the human inducible NOS:CaM holoenzyme, revealing an architecture in which the Red:CaM arm spans the Oxy dimer in an apparent active state for cross-monomer electron transfer. The flavin mononucleotide subdomain is rotated ~90° relative to the Red core, positioning its cofactor ~9 Å from the heme, adjacent to a conserved tryptophan residue within a narrow Oxy domain tunnel. Red–Oxy flexibility in the active state may facilitate electron shuttling among cofactors, defining how NOS cofactors are transiently aligned to enable catalysis. Lee et al. present the structural basis of nitric oxide synthase function, including an electron-transfer-competent state, and reveal how coordinated domain movements enable nitric oxide synthesis.

stories.title: Comparing plasma p-tau217 and plasma p-tau217/Aβ42 with CSF biomarkers for assessing Alzheimer’s disease pathology
stories.description: Plasma biomarkers for Alzheimer’s disease (AD) on fully automated platforms offer accessible, cost-effective diagnostic tools. Here we aimed to compare Lumipulse plasma phospho-tau217 (p-tau217) and the p-tau217/beta-amyloid42 ratio (p-tau217/Aβ42) with regulatory-authorized cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers (Aβ42/Aβ40 and p-tau181/Aβ42) for identifying AD pathology (Aβ-PET visual read) across a memory clinic (n = 129), a primary care (n = 220) and a research cohort (n = 165). Regulatory-authorized cutoffs were used for the plasma and CSF biomarkers. Plasma biomarkers identified Aβ pathology with areas under the curve between 0.90 and 0.96. Using one cutoff, plasma p-tau217 (83–91%) and p-tau217/Aβ42 (83–92%) had comparable accuracies to CSF (88–90%) across all cohorts (all P ≥ 0.05). With a two-cutoff approach, plasma p-tau217 (90–97%) remained comparable to CSF (91%) in the clinical cohorts (all Padj ≥ 0.12). Results with cohort-derived cutoffs are also provided. In conclusion, regulatory-authorized plasma p-tau217 and p-tau217/Aβ42 demonstrated performance comparable to regulatory-authorized CSF tests for detecting Aβ pathology in symptomatic individuals. Blood tests for Alzheimer’s disease, including regulatory authorized p-tau217 and p-tau217/AB42, are accessible and cost-effective diagnostic tools. This study shows that they perform similarly to authorized cerebrospinal fluid tests in detecting Alzheimer’s disease pathology in patients.

stories.title: Superionicity and premelting of iron-rich (Fe,Mg)O at Earth’s core-mantle boundary
stories.description: Core-mantle interactions are essential for understanding Earth’s interior dynamics and evolution. Experimental studies reveal that core-mantle reactions produce iron-rich (Fe,Mg)O (periclase‑wüstite solid solution). Here we show that Fe-rich (Fe,Mg)O exhibits pronounced superionic-onset and grain-boundary premelting behavior above ~0.9Tm (Tm: melting temperature). These effects are significant in (FexMg1-x)O (x > 0.8) under core-mantle boundary (CMB) conditions, causing elastic softening, enhanced elemental transport, and ultra-low viscosity. Enhanced diffusion may facilitate core-mantle reactions and the accumulation of Fe-rich material near the CMB, potentially contributing to a dense basal assemblage. Under mantle flow and/or thermal buoyancy, the low viscosity of connected Fe-rich (Fe,Mg)O could favor deformation and redistribution toward shallower depths. This process may contribute to the formation and evolution of some ultra-low velocity zones (ULVZs). The proposed scenario is consistent with the layered structures and inferred low viscosity of some ULVZs and suggests a potential role for Fe-rich (Fe,Mg)O in core-mantle material exchange and heat transfer. Zhang et al. find that oxygen moves rapidly through iron-rich oxides near melting, lowering viscosity and enhancing element transport at Earth’s core-mantle boundary, with implications for ultralow-velocity zones.

stories.title: GTP hydrolysis by Ras proceeds without a stabilized nucleophilic water molecule
stories.description: A comprehensive understanding of the Ras self-inactivation mechanism at atomic resolution—specifically, intrinsic GTP hydrolysis converting the GTP-bound active form to the GDP-bound inactive form—is essential for designing therapies against Ras-driven cancers. Conventional models describe a biphasic GTP-bound state: Ras interconverts between inactive state 1 and active, catalytically competent state 2. However, the structural pathway leading to Ras/GDP via these states remains unclear. Here, we use time-resolved serial femtosecond and synchrotron crystallography to capture GTP hydrolysis in Ras crystals loaded with photoactivatable caged GTP, across timescales from milliseconds to hours. Photolysis yielded Ras in state 1—a conformation lacking a stabilized nucleophilic water characteristic of state 2. Remarkably, this state persists for hours and converts directly to Ras/GDP without passing through state 2. These findings challenge the prevailing view that state 2 is essential and suggest that state 1 can directly support catalysis, offering an alternative conceptual basis for targeting clinically relevant Ras mutants that preferentially adopt this conformation. Ras proteins switch off by hydrolyzing GTP, but the structural pathway remains unclear. Here, authors use time-resolved crystallography to show that Ras can convert from state 1 directly to GDP without adopting state 2.
